A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 17 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: Sections 6–7 and Appendix D report original experiments on FB15k237 and Hetionet, including reranking comparisons and a KL-weight analysis.

after.justification: Sections 6–7 and Appendix E report original reranking experiments, parameter sensitivity results, runtime measurements and a qualitative example.

M1.justification: Section 5 replaces NQR's attention-based preference encoder and score-adjustment network with an MLP predicting weights for mean positive and negative cosine similarities. The margin-plus-KL objective becomes two RankNet terms covering preference ordering and valid-answer versus non-answer ordering. Cosine also changes from unnormalized similarity sums to an alpha/beta-weighted combination of initial scores and mean similarities.

E1.justification: Both versions use FB15k237 and Hetionet, train NQR on one-hop queries, and evaluate the same 14 query types. Dataset statistics and generated preference-set coverage match. The added qualitative example remains within the existing two-hop query task.

E2.justification: The main and appendix comparisons replace RankNet, which used v1's NQR architecture with a different loss, with a LightGBM/LambdaRank comparator. QTO remains the reference under the name Unconstrained. Cosine remains evaluated, although its procedure is revised and it becomes a proposed method.

E3.justification: V2 adds NDCG@10 with graded relevance and a runtime evaluation, and introduces LightGBM training with 100 sampled negative entities per query. Appendix E reports averaging over ten interactions, replacing v1 Appendix D's stated averaging over variable preference-set length T. The written PA rank inequality is also corrected; this does not establish that its implementation changed. Dataset splits and base-QTO settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's KL-weight investigation and same-architecture RankNet loss comparison disappear. V2 instead studies Cosine's alpha/beta trade-offs across interaction steps in Figure 4, adds a concrete reranking case study in Table 3, and measures computational overhead in Table 2.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals around the main performance curves and a paired t-test comparing Cosine and NQR runtimes. V1's multiple runs in Figure 5 vary KL weights rather than estimate stochastic uncertainty. Neither version specifies repeated-seed counts.

E6.justification: The constrained-method results are extensively replaced. Between v1 Tables 4–5 and v2 Tables 6–7, NQR's reported average MRR changes from 14.35 to 18.57 on FB15k237 and from 9.16 to 14.21 on Hetionet; its Hetionet average PA changes from 75.61 to 64.62. These involve revised methods and reported aggregation, rather than unchanged-setting gains. V2 also adds NDCG, runtime and case-study results; the appendix QTO/Unconstrained values match.

T1.justification: The FOL and interactive-query formalization is substantially retained despite the new numbered definitions. V2 revises computational-complexity derivations, adds a monotonicity argument for score updates, and corrects the PA rank comparison from greater-than in v1 Equation 8 to less-than in v2 Equation 13.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on NQR learning a preference-versus-ranking trade-off. V2 presents revised Cosine and conditional NQR as two lightweight methods, claims improving ranking performance as preferences accumulate, and emphasizes measured overhead of at most 1.4 ms. The problem and benchmark-generation contributions remain.

C2.justification: Interpretation shifts from the protective role of margin/KL training to similarity-based updates, conditional weights, and when to prefer NQR versus Cosine. V2 adds parameter-control interpretations and query-type failure cases. However, it removes v1's substantive limitations concerning missing query-structure input, constraints restricted to target variables, and the need for human validation of generated preferences.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies full-preference-set PA evaluation, frozen reused embeddings, and LightGBM feature and negative-sampling details, but drops v1's Adam/300-epoch training statement. Appendix D and Table 5 retain v1's attention architecture and margin/KL tuning information, conflicting with the revised main-text method. This leaves important implementation details unresolved.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gerritse et al. on entity retrieval, Daza et al. on text-derived entity representations, and Ke et al. on LightGBM, while removing the attention and Adam references. The learning-to-rank discussion expands around LambdaRank/LambdaMART, but the broader positioning relative to logical query answering, active learning and recommendation remains.

P1.justification: The method and results narratives are substantially rewritten and subdivided. The problem exposition gains numbered definitions and an expanded example, while the limitations section is removed. The abstract, contributions, conclusion and citation style are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template, typography and author layout, removes the NQR architecture diagram, and redesigns the main results figure with percentage axes, NDCG panels and reported confidence bands. It replaces the KL scatterplots with parameter trajectories, adds runtime and qualitative tables, and expands appendix result tables with NDCG. The dendrogram and query-type diagram are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful evidence about joint ranking quality and efficiency through NDCG, runtime measurements, parameter analyses and a concrete example. However, v1's main method and appendix agree, whereas v2 Section 5.2's conditional MLP and RankNet objectives conflict with Appendix D/Table 5's retained attention architecture and margin/KL settings. The implementation behind the new results is therefore unresolved, and substantive limitations are removed. These benefits and reproducibility and qualification regressions prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
